## Proof

**Claim:** Yes, the set $S = \{x \in [0,1] : f(x) > \sup f - \epsilon\}$ can have Lebesgue measure $0$.

**Construction.** Define $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ by
$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x = 0,\\ 0 & \text{if } x \in (0,1].\end{cases}$$
This $f$ is bounded (with $0 \le f \le 1$), and $\sup_{[0,1]} f = 1$, attained only at $x=0$.

Choose any $\epsilon$ with $0 < \epsilon < 1$. Then
$$S = \{x \in [0,1] : f(x) > 1 - \epsilon\} = \{0\},$$
since $f(0)=1 > 1-\epsilon$, while $f(x)=0 \not> 1-\epsilon$ for all $x \in (0,1]$ (as $1-\epsilon > 0$).

The set $\{0\}$ is a singleton, hence has Lebesgue measure $0$.

**Remark on non-emptiness.** Note that $S$ is always nonempty: by definition of the supremum, for every $\epsilon > 0$ there exists $x \in [0,1]$ with $f(x) > \sup f - \epsilon$. Thus $S$ cannot be empty, but—as shown above—it can nevertheless be a null set. The supremum (or near-supremum values) may be achieved on an arbitrarily small (measure-zero) subset of $[0,1]$.

**Conclusion.** There is no general lower bound on the Lebesgue measure of $S$ imposed by boundedness of $f$ alone. The set $S$ can indeed have Lebesgue measure $0$.
